name: Prefetch
location: C:\Windows\Prefetch\{EXECUTABLENAME}-{HASH}.pf. Prefetching (and therefore .pf creation) is controlled by HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management\PrefetchParameters\EnablePrefetcher, and is disabled by default on systems whose boot volume is an SSD.
purpose: Windows' prefetcher records which files and directories an executable references during its first ~10 seconds of launch, storing that data in a .pf file so future launches can be sped up by pre-loading those resources. Because a .pf file is created/updated only when the named executable actually runs, Prefetch is one of the strongest single-artifact indicators of program execution and its history (run count, run times).
key_fields: Executable name (limited to 29 characters in the filename)
Run count: total number of times the executable has been launched since the .pf file was created

Last-run timestamp, plus (format version 26 and later, i.e. Windows 8 and newer) up to 7 additional previous run timestamps for a maximum of 8 stored execution times; format version 23 (Vista/Windows 7) records only the single last-run timestamp with no run history array
Volume information: source volume path, serial number, and creation time
List of files and directories referenced during the executable's startup phase

Prefetch file format version number (17 = XP/2003, 23 = Vista/7/2008/2012, 26 = Windows 8/8.1, 30 = Windows 10). Identifies which decompression/parsing logic applies (Windows 10 .pf files are compressed and require Windows 8+ APIs to decompress)
normal_baseline: One .pf file per distinct executable path that has been run, up to a Microsoft-documented cap of 128 retained files on Windows XP/7 (oldest purged once the cap is reached) or up to 1,024 files on Windows 8 and later; run counts and run-time clusters that line up with normal user/application behavior (e.g. daily logon scripts, frequently used applications).
anomalies: A .pf file for an executable run from a Temp, Downloads, or other user-writable/unusual path, especially with a low run count consistent with a one-off tool execution
A high run count concentrated in a very short time window, consistent with automated/scripted repeated execution rather than normal interactive use
Referenced-files list inside the .pf naming unusual DLLs, staging directories, or files that no longer exist on disk. Useful for recovering paths of since-deleted malware components
A .pf file whose executable no longer exists at the referenced path (deleted post-execution) while the .pf itself remains. Direct evidence of a since-removed binary having run

Complete absence of expected Prefetch activity on a system that should have it enabled. Always confirm EnablePrefetcher's registry value and whether the boot volume is an SSD (which disables prefetching by default) before treating an empty/sparse Prefetch folder as suspicious
parsing_tools: PECmd (Eric Zimmerman): e.g. PECmd.exe -d "C:\Windows\Prefetch" --csv output-folder --csvf prefetch.csv
anti_forensic_notes: Prefetch files are ordinary files on disk (not registry-embedded), so they can be deleted individually or in bulk with simple filesystem operations. A documented anti-forensic technique corresponding to ATT&CK T1070.004 (Indicator Removal: File Deletion). Deletion of .pf files does not remove all trace, however: the NTFS Master File Table ($MFT) retains a record of the deleted file's name, size, and timestamps, and the $UsnJrnl records the deletion event itself. Because prefetching is off by default on SSD-booted systems and can be disabled entirely via EnablePrefetcher, a sparse or empty Prefetch folder is not inherently suspicious and must be evaluated against the system's actual configuration before being treated as evidence of tampering.
interpretation: Combine Prefetch with SRUM, BAM/DAM, and UserAssist for a fuller execution story. Each has different retention limits and blind spots, so the overlap is what makes the finding solid. The first-run time is only an approximation: it's derived from the .pf file's own creation time minus up to ~10 seconds, not a directly recorded field.
